title: Canopy Layers
statement: A forest survey records how many birds nest at each branch point of a tree, as a binary tree given in level order (tree), with null for a missing branch. The trunk is depth 0, its children depth 1, and so on. Return an array whose i-th entry is the total number of birds at depth i, from the trunk downward. Return an empty array for an empty tree. Counts may be negative when the survey records departures.

examples.explanation: An empty tree has no layers.

hints.content: Rebuild the tree from its level-order form first.
You need to know which nodes share a depth.
A breadth-first traversal visits the tree one layer at a time.
Keep a list of the current layer's nodes; their sum is one entry, and their non-null children form the next layer.
Stop when a layer is empty. A depth-first traversal that adds each value into sums[depth] works too.

testCases.explanation: An empty tree has no layers.
A left chain has one node per layer.
Negative counts are summed like any other.
A complete tree with four layers.

solutions.title: Sum each depth with its own traversal
solutions.intuition: For depth d, walk the whole tree and add the values found at exactly depth d.
solutions.approach: Compute the tree height. For each depth, run a recursive walk that adds a node's value when its depth matches.
solutions.pseudocode:
h = height(root); for d in 0..h-1: sums[d] = sumAt(root, d)
sumAt(node, d) = 0 if null; node.value if d == 0; else sumAt(left, d-1) + sumAt(right, d-1)
commonMistakes: Treating null placeholders as zero-valued nodes, which adds phantom layers.
Recomputing height inside the loop condition (wasteful but still correct).
solutions.interviewExplanation: Each layer gets its own traversal, so the tree is walked once per depth. That costs O(n·h), which degrades to quadratic for a chain.

solutions.title: Breadth-first, one layer at a time
solutions.intuition: BFS naturally processes all nodes of one depth before the next.
solutions.approach: Rebuild the tree. Start with the root as the current layer. Push the layer's sum, then collect the non-null children of its nodes as the next layer. Repeat until a layer is empty.
solutions.pseudocode:
layer = [root] if root else []
while layer: out.push(sum of layer values); layer = children of layer
return out
solutions.spaceComplexity: O(w) for the widest layer, plus the rebuilt tree
commonMistakes: Using a single queue without marking layer boundaries, which mixes depths.
Using shift() on a large array in a hot loop; swapping whole layer arrays avoids that cost.
solutions.interviewExplanation: I rebuild the tree and run BFS layer by layer: the sum of the current layer is one output entry, and its children form the next layer. Every node is visited once, O(n), and extra space is the widest layer. A DFS that carries depth and adds into sums[depth] gives the same result with O(h) stack instead.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.content: Layer [15, 7] sums to 22; the next layer is empty, so stop.
